DTSC 2301 · Portfolio Project 2

Down 8 After a Late Touchdown: Go for 2 or Kick?

A machine-learning win probability model, tested on ten NFL seasons (2016–2025)
Home Resume LinkedIn Project 1 Project 2

Research question: From 2016–2025, for NFL teams trailing by 8 points at the time of a try with under 10 minutes left in the 4th quarter, does attempting a 2-point conversion produce a higher expected win probability than kicking the PAT, and do observed win rates support the model's prediction?

Short answer: Yes, going for 2 is the better choice, but only slightly. In all 108 real situations, my model gave going for 2 a higher expected win probability. Real outcomes lean the same way, but there are too few games to prove it on their own.

1. Problem Definition

Picture a team trailing by 14 late in the 4th quarter. It scores a touchdown and now trails by 8, with the try still to come. The coach has two choices:

  • Kick the extra point (PAT). Almost automatic (about 94%), and it cuts the deficit to 7. But the team still needs another touchdown and another kick just to force overtime.
  • Go for 2. It works only about half the time. If it does, the deficit is 6 and the next touchdown can win the game in regulation. If it fails, the team is still down 8 but knows early that it will need another 2-pointer.

Many analysts argue that going for 2 is the smarter play, yet most coaches kicked in this spot for years. This project tests the question with data.

Prediction problem: I built a win probability (WP) model that predicts whether the team with the ball will win the game, based on the score, time, timeouts, field position and the pregame point spread. Target variable: win (1 = the team with the ball won, 0 = it lost). Task type: binary classification, where the predicted probability matters more than the yes/no label.

The model then answers the decision question by comparing the expected win probability of each choice:

E[WP | go for 2] = P(2-pt success) × WP(down 6) + P(2-pt fail) × WP(down 8)
E[WP | kick] = P(PAT success) × WP(down 7) + P(PAT miss) × WP(down 8)

Who benefits: coaches and analytics staffs making real-time calls, broadcasters explaining those calls, and fans and bettors who want to judge them fairly. Why it matters: a single late-game decision can swing a playoff race, and coaches are often judged on the outcome rather than on whether the choice was sound.

2. Background and Context

Win probability models. A WP model estimates a team's chance of winning from any game situation. Lock and Nettleton (2014) used random forests on NFL play-by-play data and found that score, time remaining, field position and the pregame betting spread drive most of the prediction. The open-source nflfastR WP model (Baldwin, 2021) adds a "score-to-time ratio" that weights the score more heavily as the clock runs down, plus a version with the pregame spread. I borrowed both ideas for my features. Yurko et al. (2019) showed how these models can be built reproducibly from public play-by-play data and used to value decisions by how much they change win probability.

Coaches are often too conservative. Romer (2006) studied 4th-down decisions and found that NFL teams kicked far more often than a win-maximizing strategy would suggest, likely because coaches fear the blame that comes with a failed aggressive call. The 2-point decision has the same structure: a safe, familiar option versus a riskier one that may be worth more.

Rule context. Before the 2015 season, the NFL moved the PAT snap back to the 15-yard line, turning it into a 33-yard kick, while 2-point tries stayed at the 2-yard line (Patra, 2015). PATs became less automatic, and going for 2 became relatively more attractive. That is why my data starts in 2016: every season uses the same rules.

Why "down 8" is the interesting case. Kicking only turns a two-step problem (touchdown plus 2-pointer) into a different two-step problem (touchdown plus kick, then overtime). Going for 2 early tells the team how many points it needs while there is still time to plan around the answer.

3. Data Description

  • Source: nflverse play-by-play data (nflverse, n.d.), the public dataset behind the nflfastR project. Files were downloaded directly from the nflverse-data GitHub releases, one per season.
  • Unit of analysis: one play, which represents one game state, seen from the perspective of the team with the ball.
  • Size: 484,254 plays from 2,761 games (2016–2025 regular season and playoffs). After cleaning: 405,821 plays × 12 features.
  • Target: win, built from each game's final score.
  • Available features: nearly 400 columns, including score, clock, down, distance, field position, timeouts, home and away teams, betting lines, play type and results. I used 12 features (see Section 5).
  • Decision dataset: the 110 tries where the scoring team trailed by 8 with under 10 minutes left in the 4th quarter. Two of those games ended in ties, which leaves 108 games: 31 went for 2 and 77 kicked.
  • Missing values: the timeout columns were missing for about 5% of rows. All of those were penalty-only or administrative rows, which I removed for other reasons, so the final table has no missing values.

Assumptions and limits on collection: the play-by-play data comes from the NFL's official game logs, so it records what happened but not why (injuries, weather, a coach's strategy). The pregame point spread is a betting-market number and only a rough stand-in for team strength.

4. Data Understanding and Exploration

Summary statistics: the average score differential is close to 0 (−1.6) with a standard deviation of 10.5 points. The pregame spread ranges from −22 to +22. Teams usually have most of their timeouts (median 3).

Target balance: the team with the ball won 50.1% of the time. Every game has one winner and one loser, and both teams have the ball about equally often, so class imbalance is not a problem for the WP model. It is a problem for the decision data, where only 31 of 108 teams went for 2.

Outliers: score differentials range from −56 to +50. These blowouts are real games, not errors, so I kept them; they help the model learn that big late leads are almost certain wins.

Conversion rates (all tries, 2016–2025): PATs succeeded 94.4% of the time (12,818 attempts) and 2-point tries succeeded 47.6% of the time (1,302 attempts). These are the probabilities in the decision formula.

How exploration shaped my approach: with only 108 decision games, training a model on those games alone would be hopeless. Instead, I trained the WP model on all 400,000+ plays, where it can learn how score, time and timeouts interact, and then applied it to the rare down-8 situation. Figure 1 also showed that the effect of the score depends on time, so I engineered features that combine the two.

5. Data Preparation and Feature Selection

Cleaning

  • Ties dropped: 10 games ended in a tie, so the target (win or lose) is undefined.
  • Overtime dropped: the research question is about regulation.
  • Try plays dropped from training: PATs and 2-point attempts are the decision I'm studying, not normal game states.
  • Penalty-only and timeout rows dropped: they repeat a neighboring play's game state, and they were the only rows with missing timeout counts.
  • Duplicates: checked on (game, play) ID; none were found.

Features

FeatureWhy it's included
Score differentialThe strongest single predictor of who wins
Time remaining (seconds)A lead matters more as time runs out
Score × time ratio (engineered)Score differential scaled up exponentially as the game goes on, following Baldwin (2021)
Pregame spread & spread × time left (engineered)Measures team strength; its influence should fade as the game goes on
Own & opponent timeoutsTimeouts stop the clock in a comeback
Home teamHome-field advantage
Down, yards to go, yards to end zone, kickoff flagField position and possession situation

Deliberately excluded: nflfastR's own wp and vegas_wp columns (another model's answers), final scores and game results (which are the answer), and anything measured after the play. Using any of these would be data leakage.

Encoding and scaling: for logistic regression, numeric features were standardized and down was one-hot encoded, since 4th down isn't simply "1 more" than 3rd down. Tree models don't need scaling. All scaling was fit inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so test data never influenced it.

Train/test split and leakage prevention

  • Split by season, not by random rows: train on 2016–2022 (281,581 plays, 1,897 games) and test on 2023–2025 (124,240 plays, 854 games). Plays from the same game share one outcome, so a random split would put near-copies of test games into training and inflate the scores.
  • The split also tests time: strategy changed a lot after 2022 (Figure 2), so a model that still works on 2023–2025 is more trustworthy.
  • Tuning used only training seasons, with 3-fold cross-validation grouped by game.
  • Leave-one-season-out predictions for the 108 decision games: each game was scored by a model that never saw its season.

6. Baseline and Model Development

  • Baseline: predict the average win rate (about 50%) for every play. This is what you'd guess knowing nothing about the game situation, so any useful model must beat it.
  • Model 1: Logistic regression. A simple, interpretable model that turns a weighted sum of features into a probability. It assumes win probability changes smoothly with each feature.
  • Model 2: Gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn HistGradientBoostingClassifier). It can learn complicated interactions between score, time and timeouts on its own. I added monotonic constraints so that win probability can only go up as a team's lead or pregame spread improves.

Hyperparameter tuning: I tested 12 combinations of learning rate (0.05, 0.1), tree size (15, 31, 63 leaves) and regularization (0, 1) using game-grouped cross-validation on the training seasons. The best combination was learning rate 0.05, 15 leaves and regularization 1.0 (CV log loss 0.446).

Fair comparison: every model used the same features, the same training seasons and the same held-out test seasons, and was scored with the same metrics.

7. Model Evaluation and Selection

Because the final step plugs the model's probabilities into a formula, I chose metrics that judge probability quality, not just whether the model picked the right winner:

  • Log loss: punishes confident wrong predictions heavily. Lower is better; a coin flip scores 0.693.
  • Brier score (Brier, 1950): the average squared gap between predicted probability and outcome. Lower is better; a coin flip scores 0.25.
  • ROC AUC: how well the model ranks winners above losers (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect). It ignores calibration, so it's a secondary metric here.

I also scored the subset that matters most: late-game plays (4th quarter, under 10 minutes).

Model (test seasons 2023–2025)Log lossBrierAUCLate log lossLate Brier
Baseline (always ~50%)0.6930.2500.5000.6930.250
Logistic regression ✓ final model0.4500.1490.8670.2830.090
Gradient boosting (tuned)0.4540.1510.8640.2830.090
Reference: nflfastR vegas_wp (professional model)0.4480.1480.8680.2720.087

Both models crushed the baseline, cutting log loss by about 35% overall and by about 60% late in games. Both came close to the professionally built nflfastR model, which I scored only as a benchmark, never as an input.

The deciding test: is the model's answer stable?

The two models were essentially tied on standard metrics, so I added a test aimed at the research question itself. The decision depends on tiny differences between the win probability of being down 6, 7 or 8. A model can be accurate overall and still get those differences wrong. I resampled whole games 25 times (a bootstrap), refit each model, and recomputed the go-for-2 advantage each time.

Why the models behave differently: the boosted model divides the score into bins wherever that helps overall accuracy. Late-game kickoffs with a 6-, 7- or 8-point lead are a tiny slice of the data, so the exact bin edges near those margins shift with every resample. That is noise, not football knowledge. Logistic regression assumes a smooth relationship, which keeps its answer steady.

Final model: logistic regression. It matched or beat gradient boosting on every held-out metric, it is well calibrated in the late-game region, it is easy to interpret, and it is the only model that gives a stable answer to the research question.

The trade-off: a smooth model can't capture football's "key numbers," for example that being down 7 is a different situation from being down 8 because of the 2-point try. I checked how much this matters in Section 8.

Errors are largest early in close games, where anything can still happen, and smallest late in lopsided ones. The down-8 decision sits in the "one-score, 2–10 minutes" zone: the model is useful there, but a lot of real uncertainty remains. That uncertainty comes from football itself, not from a flaw in the model.

Answering the research question

Across the 108 real situations, the model favored going for 2 every time. The average expected win probability was 7.2% if going for 2 vs. 6.9% if kicking: a gain of +0.25 percentage points, or about a 4% relative improvement in a team's chances.

Sanity check: what does the raw data say?

Because the smooth model can't see "key numbers," I also looked at the raw data with no model: how often did a team that kicked off late in the 4th quarter come back to win?

Trailing byLate kickoffsCame back to win95% intervalModel's estimate
6 points9911.1%6.3–18.8%9.4%
7 points1987.1%4.3–11.5%7.1%
8 points1277.1%3.8–12.9%5.4%

In the raw data, being down 7 was no better than being down 8, while being down 6 was clearly better. Plugged into the same formula, these raw rates give 9.0% for going for 2 vs. 7.1% for kicking, a much bigger edge than my model's. If the raw pattern is even roughly right, my model's recommendation is conservative: going for 2 is likely worth more than the model says. The intervals are wide and teams don't land in these spots at random, so this is a sanity check, not proof.

Do observed win rates support the model?

  • The model rated the go-for-2 teams' situations as slightly worse on average (6.3% vs. 7.3%), yet those teams won more often. If anything, the real outcomes lean even more toward going for 2 than the model does.
  • Of the 31 teams that went for 2, 18 converted (58%). Teams that converted won 17% of the time; teams that failed won 8%.
  • Across all 108 games, the model predicted 7.0% wins and teams actually won 10.2% (11 of 108), which is inside the range expected from random chance at this sample size.

What we can conclude: the model says going for 2 is slightly better, the break-even math says it holds up even for a weak 2-point offense, and the real outcomes are consistent with that.

What we can't conclude: the observed win rates can't prove the model right by themselves. With 31 attempts, a difference of a few percentage points is impossible to separate from luck. The model also shows association in historical game states, not a controlled experiment.

9. Limitations, Ethics, and Reflection

Limitations and possible bias

  • Small decision sample: only 108 real games fit the situation, so the observed-win-rate check has very little statistical power.
  • Selection bias: coaches don't choose at random. Teams that went for 2 may have had better offenses, more aggressive coaches or different opponents. Observed win rates mix the effect of the choice with the effect of who made it.
  • The smooth model misses key numbers: logistic regression can't represent the special jump between being down 7 and down 8. The raw data suggests this makes my estimate too small, not too large.
  • League-average conversion rates: I used 47.6% for 2-pointers and 94.4% for PATs. A team with an elite short-yardage offense, or a shaky kicker, faces different numbers.
  • Changing league: new kickoff rules in 2024–2025 and the rise of aggressive coaching mean the game in 2016 is not identical to the game in 2025.
  • Missing context: injuries, weather, momentum and play-calling tendencies aren't in the data.

Consequences of wrong predictions

  • If the model wrongly says "go for 2" and the try fails, the coach takes public blame and, in the worst case, it costs a playoff spot or a job. Because the edge is small, being wrong in this direction costs little in expected terms. But the cost lands on people: coaches, players and their reputations.
  • If the model wrongly says "kick," the team quietly gives up a small amount of win probability. This mistake is invisible, which is exactly why coaches drifted toward it for years (Romer, 2006).

Would I use this for real decisions?

As one input, yes: it gives a clear, transparent default backed by ten seasons of data. As the only input, no. A real staff should adjust for its own 2-point success rate, its kicker, the opponent, and the specific clock and timeout situation. Users should understand that a +0.25 point edge means "slightly better on average over many games," not "this will work tonight." Win probability models can also shape betting markets and public criticism of coaches, so results should always be presented with their uncertainty.

What I'd explore next

  • A drive-level simulation that models each remaining possession, which would capture key numbers directly.
  • Team-specific 2-point success rates using offensive and defensive strength in short yardage.
  • Expanding to related decisions (down 2, down 5, down 15) and to college football.
  • A propensity-score approach to compare similar teams that made different choices, to reduce selection bias.

10. Code and Transparency

Jupyter Notebook GitHub Repository

The notebook downloads the data automatically, runs every step top to bottom, and saves every chart on this page. The 108 decision situations with model predictions are saved in data/nfl_down8_tries_2016_2025.csv. Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), SciPy and Matplotlib.

Code excerpts from the analysis notebook

These excerpts show the situation filter, logistic regression pipeline, and expected-win-probability calculation. They use variables and helper functions defined in the full notebook linked above.

Select late-game tries while trailing by eight

tries = df[((df.extra_point_attempt == 1) | (df.two_point_attempt == 1))
           & (df.qtr == 4) & (df.game_seconds_remaining < 600)
           & (df.score_differential == -8) & (df.result != 0)].copy()

Build and fit the logistic regression pipeline

num_cols = [c for c in FEATURES if c != "down"]
def make_logit():
    return Pipeline([
        ("prep", ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), num_cols),
                                    ("down", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["down"])])),
        ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=1.0)),
    ])
logit = make_logit().fit(X_tr, y_tr)

Compare going for two with kicking the PAT

def expected_wp(model, state, p2=p_2pt, pk=p_pat):
    wp6, wp7, wp8 = (trailing_wp(model, lead, **state) for lead in (6, 7, 8))
    go2 = p2 * wp6 + (1 - p2) * wp8
    kick = pk * wp7 + (1 - pk) * wp8
    breakeven = pk * (wp7 - wp8) / (wp6 - wp8)
    return go2, kick, breakeven, wp6, wp7, wp8
